item.research_question: How can the design principles of metastable β-Ti alloys be converged with high-entropy/medium-entropy alloys to achieve both high yield strength and low elastic modulus for biomedical implants?
item.material_system: Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta-Mo, Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta, Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Ta, Ti-V-Mo, Ti-V-Zr-Mo, and Ti-rich variants (e.g., Ti65-Zr20-Nb10-Mo5, Ti35-Zr27.5-Hf27.5-Nb5-Ta5)
item.processing_route: Casting (as-cast), annealing (e.g., 1000 °C for 168 h), and thermodynamic simulation using FactSage, Pandat, and Thermo-Calc to adjust compositions for phase stability and segregation reduction
item.test_conditions: Potentiodynamic polarization in simulated body fluid, compression and tensile testing, cell culture tests (osteoblasts), X-ray diffraction (XRD), SAED-TEM, and EPMA-WDS mapping
key_findings: Equiatomic Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta-Mo HEA exhibited a compressive yield strength of 1330 MPa but suffered from severe dendritic segregation and a high elastic modulus.
Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta MEA (quaternary) achieved a compressive strain of 48 ± 6% and yield strength >1000 MPa, surpassing Ti-6Al-4V (970 MPa).
Ti65-Zr20-Nb10-Mo5 alloy showed the lowest elastic modulus (86 GPa) among Ti-rich MEAs and a yield strength of 1381 MPa.
Metastable Ti65-Zr18-Nb16-Mo1 ([Mo]eq ≈ 10) achieved high yield strength (>1100 MPa) and a lower elastic modulus (~60 GPa).
Ti45-Zr45-Nb5-Ta5 MEA (VEC = 4.18) exhibited a low elastic modulus of 57 GPa.
Increasing Ti content in Tix-Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEAs increased yield strength by 31% (Ti1 vs Ti0.25) and improved compressive deformability.
Ti1.4-Zr1.4-Nb0.6-Ta0.6-Mo0.6 HEA showed osteoblasts with more pseudopodia and longer focal adhesions compared to commercially pure Ti.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that reducing the valence electron concentration (VEC) to 4.0–4.2 or the Mo equivalent ([Mo]eq) to below 10 wt% induces a metastable β-phase, which lowers the elastic modulus. Simultaneously, the high-entropy effects (lattice distortion, solid solution strengthening) and Ti-rich compositions enhance yield strength. Reducing the atomic size misfit (δ) and mixing enthalpy (ΔHmix) near zero minimizes compositional segregation and prevents intermetallic formation, thereby improving ductility and corrosion resistance.
item.limitations: Severe compositional segregation persists in many equiatomic and non-equiatomic HEAs/MEAs, leading to high elastic modulus, reduced ductility, and decreased corrosion resistance. The Ms theory may not be applicable to HEAs/MEAs, and some alloys with high Ti content still exhibit segregation. The presence of Laves phases or secondary BCC phases can adversely affect mechanical properties.
item.future_work: Developing metastable β HEAs/MEAs that combine high strength and low modulus; surface modification of Ti-containing HEAs to induce bioactivity (e.g., anodization, hydroxyapatite deposition); further investigation into the relationship between thermodynamic parameters and modulus; and reducing segregation through optimized composition design.
quotes: To satisfy the demands of biomedical implants, researchers have sought to synthesize the strengths of high-entropy alloys and metastable β-Ti alloys, culminating in the development of metastable high-entropy/medium-entropy alloys that manifest both high strength and a low elastic modulus.
When the VEC value of the alloy is approximately 4.2–4.24, the alloy can reach the BCC metastable state and obtain a lower elastic modulus.
Reducing the alloy's δ value significantly minimized compositional segregation, a highly favorable aspect for subsequent processing.
